vulnerabilities.title: DAY SEVEN AND NOTHING HAS CHANGED, WHICH IS THE UPDATE: Azure API Management Classic Still Has No CVE, No Public Advisory, No Customer-Visible Log and No Way to Prove You Were Not Accessed - Microsoft's Fix Explicitly Does Not Invalidate Credentials Already Stolen, So the Only Measurable Thing Is How Far Through Rotation You Have Got
affected_products: Azure API Management Classic - Developer tier
Azure API Management Classic - Basic tier
Azure API Management Classic - Standard tier
Azure API Management Classic - Premium tier
NOT affected: Consumption Classic and all v2 tiers
vulnerabilities.summary:
This was rank 1 yesterday. It is rank 7 today not because it has become less serious but because two items with dated KEV deadlines and one with a near-universal reachable attack surface arrived above it. Nothing about the exposure has improved, and the specific update after a week is that nothing has been published: still no CVE, still no publicly readable advisory, still no customer-visible log, and no new detection path from Microsoft or from any third party in this window. For an item of this consequence, a week of silence is itself the finding.

WHAT HAPPENED. Attackers exploited a flaw in the Azure API Management management plane to read customer secrets out of APIM Classic instances. The reported exposure list is specific and bad: Named Values, including the ones holding database credentials, service account passwords and signing keys; identity provider and OpenID Connect client secrets; subscription keys; and direct management API tokens. Microsoft identified the issue on 18 November 2026 and closed the path on 19 November 2026. Affected tiers are Developer, Basic, Standard and Premium Classic. Consumption Classic and all v2 tiers are not affected.

THE THREE FACTS THAT LEAVE NO WAY OUT, AND THEY HAVE NOT CHANGED. First, Microsoft has stated plainly that the fix does NOT invalidate credentials already stolen. The path is closed; whatever left through it is still valid until you rotate it. Second, the exploited API produced no customer-visible logging, so you cannot confirm access and you cannot rule it out - there is no query in this report or anywhere else that answers 'were we accessed'. Third, the advisory, reportedly identified as MZK9-GH0, is not public: it is visible only in your own Azure Service Health blade, which means you cannot read your neighbour's copy, your auditor cannot read yours, and no amount of searching substitutes for logging into the portal and looking.

THE UK GOVERNMENT ANGLE. Norway's national cyber security authority NSM has publicly tied this flaw to attacks on its energy sector, and its guidance is to assume exposure and rotate. That is a NATO ally's national authority treating this as a critical national infrastructure matter, which is the strongest external signal available to a UK public body weighing whether rotation is proportionate. There is no equivalent UK publication: no NCSC alert on this specific issue surfaced in this run. APIM sits in front of a great many UK government and NHS integration layers precisely because it is the component that holds the credentials for everything behind it, which is what makes the Named Values exposure the serious part - it is not one secret, it is the index of secrets.

WHAT TO DO, AND IT IS STILL ONLY ONE THING. Rotate. In order: Named Values holding database credentials, service account passwords and signing keys first; then identity provider and OpenID Connect client secrets; then subscription keys; then management API tokens. There is no detection-based alternative and no partial measure that reduces the risk, because the credentials are either still valid or they are not.

THE ONE THING THAT WILL OUTLAST THIS INCIDENT. Rotation forces you to build a map of which Named Value feeds which backend dependency. Almost no organisation has that map, and its absence is why rotation is slow and frightening rather than routine. Keep it. It is the most valuable artefact that will come out of this incident, and it is the thing that will make the next credential exposure a day of work instead of a week.

EVIDENCE QUALITY, UNCHANGED AND IMPORTANT. Everything in this entry derives from secondary reporting of a non-public Microsoft advisory and of NSM's advisory. No primary source has been read. The exposed-secret list and the statement that the fix does not invalidate stolen credentials are consistently reported across sources but could not be verified at origin. There is no CVE, so this item will not appear in your vulnerability scanner, your patch compliance report or your KEV tracker - which means that if your process only acts on things with CVE identifiers, this one is invisible to it by construction. That is the structural lesson worth taking from a week of this entry sitting in the report.
recommended_actions: If you have not already, establish today whether you run Azure API Management Classic in Developer, Basic, Standard or Premium tier. Consumption Classic and all v2 tiers are not affected. This is a five-minute check in the portal or via the resource SKU, and it is the only question that decides whether the rest of this applies.

Open the Azure Service Health blade in each affected subscription and read the advisory, reportedly MZK9-GH0, for yourself. It is not published anywhere else. Searching the web for it, including reading this report, is not a substitute - and your auditor will need the portal screenshot, not a news article.

Rotate in this order: Named Values holding database credentials, service account passwords and signing keys; then identity provider and OpenID Connect client secrets; then subscription keys; then management API tokens. There is no detection-based alternative, because Microsoft has stated the fix does not invalidate credentials already stolen.

Track rotation completion as a percentage and report it weekly. This is the only measurable thing in this entry. There is no scan result, no patch level and no log query that produces a status, so rotation progress is the status.

Build and KEEP the map of which Named Value feeds which backend dependency. Rotation forces you to construct it; almost no organisation has it in advance, and its absence is the entire reason rotation is slow. It is the most valuable durable output of this incident.

Do not wait for a CVE. There is none, and the absence means this item will never appear in your vulnerability scanner, your patch compliance report or your KEV tracker. If your remediation process only acts on CVE identifiers, add a route for vendor incidents that do not carry one.

Review which identities held APIM management API tokens and reduce that set while you rotate. A management token is the broadest credential in the exposed list and the one least likely to have a documented owner.

Where you cannot rotate a credential quickly - a signing key with downstream dependencies, a database credential in a legacy integration - document the exposure and the date, and put compensating monitoring on the backend it protects. An undocumented un-rotated credential is the one that will still be valid in six months.

Cite Norway's NSM guidance when making the case internally. A NATO ally's national authority has tied this flaw to attacks on its energy sector and advises assuming exposure and rotating. No equivalent UK publication surfaced in this run, so NSM is the strongest external authority available.

Record explicitly that you cannot determine whether you were accessed, and get that accepted at the right level rather than leaving it implicit. The exploited API produced no customer-visible logging. 'We found no evidence of access' is a misleading statement here, because no evidence of access could exist either way.

vulnerabilities.title: BOTH DEADLINES HAVE NOW EXPIRED AND THE HUNTING HAS NOT: Cisco Expressway CVE-2026-76466 and BroadWorks CVE-2026-20320 - One Command Against erlang.log Is Still the Hardest Indicator in This Report, the Expressway Intrusion Reached Internal GitLab Repositories, and Patching Neither Appliance Undoes What Was Disclosed
affected_products: Cisco Expressway - clustered nodes, fixed in X15.5.20
Cisco BroadWorks Open Client Interface - fixed in RI.2026.07
Cisco TelePresence Video Communication Server deployments sharing the Expressway code base
vulnerabilities.summary:
Both KEV deadlines in this entry have now passed - BroadWorks CVE-2026-20320 expired on 24 November and the Expressway item earlier. Nothing in the remediation closes with the deadline, and the two actions that matter most are still outstanding in most estates: one log search, and one credential audit that has nothing to do with the appliance.

THE ONE COMMAND. Search erlang.log on every Cisco Expressway node for a nodeup event from wombat@127.0.0.1. That string remains the single hardest indicator in this report - the only concrete, searchable, non-behavioural artefact across ten entries. It comes from F6's account of a real intrusion and it is reported consistently across multiple secondary accounts, though no primary source could be read. If you do nothing else from this entry, do that, because it takes one command and it either finds something or it does not.

WHAT THE EXPRESSWAY INTRUSION ACTUALLY DID, AND WHY THE APPLIANCE IS THE SMALL PART. F6's account, now corroborated across multiple secondary reports, describes four devices compromised and then post-intrusion activity that moved immediately off the appliance: custom Python scripts scanning for SMB, SQL Server and WinRM, and searching internal GitLab repositories for credentials. Read that last clause again, because it determines the scope of your response. An attacker who reaches a video conferencing appliance and then harvests credentials out of internal source control has acquired something that survives every patch you apply to the appliance. If you upgrade Expressway to X15.5.20, block TCP 4371 to 4372, treat every cluster peer as compromised where any node was reachable - all correct - and do not audit internal GitLab and rotate what you find there, you have closed the door and left the keys outside it.

F6 additionally assessed that the post-intrusion Python tooling was likely written with an AI assistant. That is an inference from code characteristics, it is single-source, and it is recorded here as such - but it is also one of the five AI-agent-adjacent reports that drove last week's analysis and that the NCSC publication at rank 5 now describes in general terms.

BROADWORKS, WHERE THE DEADLINE EXPIRED YESTERDAY. CVE-2026-20320 is an unauthenticated XML external entity flaw in the BroadWorks Open Client Interface on TCP 2208. It reads arbitrary files from the server, including configuration files containing keys. Cisco disclosed it on 19 August 2026, so the fix - RI.2026.07 - has existed for three months. Malbear Labs reported that an AI agent exploited this flaw against a telecommunications provider; that is a single-source claim and is labelled as such. Two actions: block TCP 2208 at the perimeter and upgrade; and rotate the keys that were in the configuration files, because file disclosure is not undone by a patch. The practical obstacle in most organisations is ownership - BroadWorks is a carrier voice platform, it is usually run by a voice or unified communications team, and that team is frequently outside the security patching process entirely. Find out today who owns it. In a number of UK public bodies the answer will be a managed service provider, which turns this into the same written-question exercise as rank 3.

THE VENDOR-VERSUS-AUTHORITY SPLIT, WHICH IS NOW A STANDING FEATURE. Cisco's PSIRT position is that it is not aware of active exploitation in the wild for CVE-2026-76466, and that it lacks direct evidence of exploitation for CVE-2026-20320. CISA has both in KEV. F6 reports first-hand incident response on the Expressway flaw. This is not a contradiction to resolve so much as a structural characteristic of vendor advisories: a PSIRT states what it has verified itself, and an incident responder states what it saw at a customer. Prioritise on the KEV listing and the first-hand account, and expect your vulnerability management tooling - which usually ingests the vendor statement - to disagree. That disagreement appeared five times in a single day last week and twice more in today's report.

WHAT IS STILL MISSING. No file hashes, no YARA rules, no malware sample references and no command-and-control infrastructure have been published for either flaw. Everything except wombat@127.0.0.1 and the port numbers is behavioural or structural. Neither Cisco advisory nor F6's report could be read directly in this run.
recommended_actions: Run the one command today: search erlang.log on every Cisco Expressway node for a nodeup event from wombat@127.0.0.1. It is the hardest indicator in this report, it takes one command, and it is the highest value-per-minute action available across all ten entries.

Audit internal GitLab and other source control for committed credentials, and rotate everything you find. This is the action most likely to be skipped and the one that determines whether the intrusion is actually closed, because post-intrusion tooling in the Expressway case specifically searched repositories for credentials - and those credentials survive every appliance patch.

Upgrade clustered Expressway nodes to X15.5.20 and block TCP 4371 to 4372 at the perimeter. Treat every cluster peer as compromised if any node in the cluster was externally reachable, rather than only the node you have evidence for.

Block TCP 2208 at the perimeter and upgrade BroadWorks to RI.2026.07. Cisco disclosed CVE-2026-20320 on 19 August 2026, so the fix has been available for three months and the KEV deadline expired yesterday - record the date you act, because the compliance position is already overdue.

Rotate every key that was present in BroadWorks configuration files. The flaw reads arbitrary files including configuration containing keys. Patching stops further disclosure; it does not un-disclose what was already read.

Find out today who owns your BroadWorks estate, and expect the answer to be a voice or unified communications team outside the security patching process, or a managed service provider. This ownership gap, not the technical difficulty, is why a three-month-old fix is still unapplied in most organisations.

Hunt for internal reconnaissance from the appliances themselves: SMB, SQL Server and WinRM scanning originating from Expressway or BroadWorks hosts. That is the documented post-intrusion behaviour and it is detectable in network telemetry even without indicators.

Expect your vulnerability management tooling to disagree with this entry and override it. Cisco PSIRT states it is not aware of exploitation for CVE-2026-76466 and lacks direct evidence for CVE-2026-20320, while CISA lists both in KEV and F6 reports first-hand incident response. Prioritise on KEV and the first-hand account.

Record the expired deadlines explicitly rather than letting them drop off the tracker. Both are now overdue, and an item that silently disappears from a KEV report when its date passes is the most common way overdue remediation becomes invisible.

Review which other appliances in your estate hold credentials for internal systems in their configuration, and whether anyone has ever audited what an attacker reading those files would obtain. Expressway and BroadWorks are instances of a category: network appliances trusted enough to hold keys and excluded from the patching process that protects them.

kql.name: Internal reconnaissance originating from voice and conferencing appliances

kql.name: Internal source control access and repository enumeration
kql.description: The action most likely to be skipped. Post-intrusion tooling searched internal GitLab for credentials, so this looks for the enumeration pattern - one identity reading many repositories in a short window.
kql.query:
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > datetime(2026-08-01)
| where Application has_any ("GitLab", "GitHub", "Bitbucket", "Azure DevOps")
| where ActionType has_any ("Read", "Clone", "Download", "Search", "FileAccessed", "RepositoryAccessed")
| summarize Actions = count(), Objects = dcount(ObjectName), Repos = make_set(ObjectName, 40) by AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, bin(Timestamp, 1h)
| where Objects >= 15
| order by Objects desc

kql.name: Credential search patterns in source trees and configuration
kql.description: The tooling behaviour rather than the tool. An attacker or an agent searching for credentials uses recognisable patterns, and these are cheap to detect because legitimate use is rare on servers.
kql.query:
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > datetime(2026-08-01)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("grep -r", "findstr /s", "Select-String", "rg ")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("password", "passwd", "secret", "api_key", "apikey", "token", "BEGIN RSA", "BEGIN PRIVATE", "connectionstring", ".env", "credentials")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc

kql.name: Cisco Expressway and BroadWorks build verification
kql.description: Produces the remediation evidence for two expired KEV deadlines. Cross-check against X15.5.20 for Expressway and RI.2026.07 for BroadWorks rather than against change tickets.

| where SyslogMessage has_any ("Expressway", "BroadWorks", "VCS", "X15.", "RI.2026", "Open Client Interface")

| where isnotempty(ExpresswayVersion) or isnotempty(BroadWorksRelease)
| summarize LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Versions = make_set(ExpresswayVersion, 5), Releases = make_set(BroadWorksRelease, 5) by Computer
| order by Computer asc

vulnerabilities.title: THE UK CORPORATE PATTERN THIS MONTH, AND IT IS NOT ABOUT ANY ONE COMPANY: Next, ASOS, Optimizely and Five Leak-Site Listings - in EVERY Confirmed UK Retail and Consumer Disclosure This Month the Compromise Was at a Third Party, Not at the Named Brand, Which Means the Control That Would Have Prevented Them Is Supplier Assurance Rather Than Anything in Your Own Estate
vulnerabilities.vendor: Multiple - UK retail, consumer and healthcare supply chain
affected_products: Third-party online suppliers to UK retailers
Third-party customer communication and marketing platforms
Third-party experimentation and analytics JavaScript
Managed service providers supplying UK public sector and SME organisations
vulnerabilities.summary:
Taken individually these are small items. Taken together they are the clearest finding in this report about UK corporate risk, and it is a finding about architecture rather than about any of the companies named.

NEXT PLC, 23 NOVEMBER, COVERAGE CONTINUING THROUGH 24 NOVEMBER. Next disclosed that a third-party online supplier suffered a cyber incident in which an unauthorised party gained access to some data relating to Next. Next's position is that its own systems were not compromised, that current evidence indicates no customer personal data was compromised, and that the affected information is benign and cannot be used to facilitate fraud against customers or the company. The supplier has not been named and the data has not been described. Next is working with the supplier, law enforcement and regulatory authorities. The share price dipped on the news and recovered the same day to trade slightly up. This is a well-handled disclosure - prompt, specific about what is and is not known, and clear about the limits of current evidence - and it should be read as the benchmark rather than as a failure.

ASOS, DISCLOSED OCTOBER, INVESTIGATION CONCLUDED EARLY NOVEMBER. ASOS told the London Stock Exchange that a third-party platform used for customer communication was compromised, and that users consequently received unauthorised push notifications - one of which read as a ransom demand claiming the attackers had fully compromised a Snowflake instance and threatening to leak it. Snowflake has stated that its own systems were not breached. ASOS's conclusion was that basic customer data including names and contact details was accessed, and that payment card information and account passwords were not. BBC reporting, relayed via TechCrunch, indicates the exposed data may also include home addresses, telephone numbers, email addresses and notes in customer profiles including website search queries - that broader list is NOT confirmed by ASOS and should not be treated as established. The actor self-identifies as Xuanye Group. The NCSC advised ASOS customers to assume they were affected even if they received no notification, which is the right default and worth borrowing as a communications pattern. One account links the compromised platform to a marketing product running on Snowflake Cortex AI; that is single-source and unconfirmed. Accounts also differ on whether the entry was a vendor compromise or an employee account, and that is unresolved.

AND RANK 2 OF THIS REPORT IS THE SAME SHAPE. The Optimizely compromise reached at least 178 organisations through attacker-controlled JavaScript served from the vendor's own CDN. Nobody's own estate was breached. The script was authorised, allowlisted, served over TLS from the expected host.

LEAK-SITE AND TRACKER ACTIVITY, WITH THE APPROPRIATE SCEPTICISM. UK names appearing on leak sites and breach trackers this month include Bensons for Beds Retail, listed by N0n on 17 November; Audio Note UK Ltd, listed by Osiris on 11 November; Fittleworth, a UK healthcare company providing home delivery of medical supplies, recorded with a discovery date of 20 November; and Simply UK, Ion Asset Architecture and William Cook. Gnosis Pay, a London payments firm, reported a breach on 3 November. N0n claimed three further anonymised UK entries on 23 November, and the BYOD group posted its most recent victim on 24 November with the country not visible in available sources. Ransomware.live's running UK total stands at 1,209 victims. The Fittleworth listing is the one to watch from a UK government perspective: medical supply home delivery sits in the NHS supply chain and holds patient-identifiable data by necessity.

THE CAVEATS ARE NOT DECORATIVE. Every leak-site item above is attacker self-reporting and none of the named organisations has confirmed an incident in the sources reviewed. Bitdefender has documented N0n inflating its victim count by roughly a factor of five, and tracker totals vary by around seventy victims depending on collection method. RedPacket Security has specifically warned that listings attributed to Aurora have included unverified or fabricated victim claims. Treat these as leads for supplier enquiry, not as facts about those companies.

THE FINDING. Across every confirmed UK retail and consumer disclosure this month, the compromise was at a third party and not at the named brand. Next: a supplier. ASOS: a communications platform. Optimizely: a vendor's CDN. N-able Mail Assure at rank 3: a vendor's hosted platform, reaching UK organisations through MSPs. That is four for four. No amount of hardening inside your own perimeter addresses any of them. The controls that do are an inventory of which third parties can reach your data or execute code in your users' browsers, contractual notification obligations with hours attached, and the ability to answer 'what would we lose if this vendor were compromised' before rather than after. And that is the same inventory the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill's vendor-direction powers at rank 10 will require of regulated bodies - which makes building it now the one action in this report that satisfies both an immediate risk and a known future obligation.
recommended_actions: Build the third-party inventory that four out of four incidents this month point at: every vendor that holds your customer data, that can send messages to your customers in your name, or that executes JavaScript in your users' browsers. Most organisations have the first list, few have the second, and almost none have the third - which is the one that produced rank 2 of this report.

For each third party on that list, answer in writing what you would lose if it were compromised, and do it before the incident. The question is unanswerable in the first forty-eight hours of a real event, which is exactly when it gets asked.

Review your contractual notification obligations with suppliers and attach hours to them. Next learned of its supplier's incident in time to disclose promptly; that is the outcome the contract should guarantee rather than something to hope for.

Borrow the NCSC's communications pattern from the ASOS incident: advise customers to assume they were affected even if they received no notification. It is the honest default when a third-party platform's logs cannot establish which individuals were reached, and it avoids the position of having to broaden the statement later.

Ask your marketing and digital teams directly which third-party scripts run on your public web properties, and specifically which run on authentication and payment pages. Do not ask IT - these products are procured by marketing, which is precisely why they are absent from the asset register.

Treat the Fittleworth listing as a supply-chain enquiry if you are an NHS body. Medical supply home delivery holds patient-identifiable data by necessity and sits in the NHS supply chain. The listing is unconfirmed attacker self-reporting, which makes it a reason to ask, not a reason to conclude.

Do not act on leak-site listings as established fact about any named company. Bitdefender has documented N0n inflating victim counts roughly fivefold, tracker totals vary by about seventy victims by collection method, and RedPacket Security warns that Aurora-attributed listings have included fabricated claims. Use them to open a conversation with a supplier, not to make a determination.

Specifically do not repeat the broader ASOS data list as established. ASOS confirmed names and contact details. The additional items - home addresses, telephone numbers, email addresses and profile notes including search queries - come from BBC reporting and are not confirmed by ASOS. Mixing them produces a statement you may have to retract.

Add a question to your supplier assurance process that none of these incidents would have survived: can you tell us not only when your systems were accessed, but what was taken or captured? Optimizely's honest answer - that it can see when the injected code loaded but not what it captured - is the answer most vendors would have to give and almost none volunteer.

Start the third-party criticality inventory now rather than after the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill completes its passage. The vendor-direction powers in clauses 44 to 47 are already settled, most UK public bodies cannot currently state which suppliers sit in their critical path, and this is the one action in this report that addresses both a present risk and a known future obligation.

kql.name: Third-party OAuth applications and service principals with access to your data
kql.description: Produces the inventory that four out of four incidents this month point at. Every entry is a vendor that can reach your data without compromising your perimeter, and the ones nobody recognises are the finding.
kql.query:
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(90d)
| where ActionType has_any ("Consent to application", "Add service principal", "Add app role assignment", "Add OAuth2PermissionGrant", "Update application")
| extend App = tostring(RawEventData.Target[0].ID), Actor = tostring(RawEventData.UserId)
| project Timestamp, Application, ActionType, Actor, App, IPAddress, ObjectName, RawEventData
| order by Timestamp desc

kql.name: Supplier, partner and MSP identities authenticating into your tenant
kql.description: The access path that supplier compromise actually uses. Review the list for accounts belonging to engagements that have ended, which are the ones nobody will notice being used.

SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
| where UserType == "Guest" or UserPrincipalName has_any ("#EXT#", "supplier", "partner", "vendor", "msp", "contractor", "consult")
| summarize Signins = count(), Successes = countif(ResultType == 0), Apps = make_set(AppDisplayName, 20), IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 20), Countries = make_set(Location, 10), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by UserPrincipalName

| where Timestamp > datetime(2026-11-01)
| where Subject has_any ("data breach", "security incident", "your account", "unauthorised access", "unauthorized access", "supplier", "reset your password", "verify your account")
   or SenderFromDomain has_any ("next", "asos", "optimizely")
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound"

vulnerabilities.title: UK GOVERNANCE AND THE EXPIRED-DEADLINE BOARD: The Commons Reportedly Disagreed With Both Lords Amendments to the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill Yesterday, Sending It Back to the Lords With No Royal Assent and a Carry-Over to April 2027 - and One Month On, Nobody Has Published Whether the 32 UK Government Services Taken Offline for the PHP Flaw Are Back

vulnerabilities.summary:
Two governance items, one legislative and one that is a month old and has gone quiet, plus the board of expired deadlines this report is now carrying.

THE CYBER SECURITY AND RESILIENCE BILL. The Commons was due to consider the Lords amendments on 24 November 2026. A single non-official source - a Bill-tracking website - records that the Commons disagreed with both Lords defeats: the register of foreign powers by 260 votes to 98, and the NIS review amendment without a division. If that is accurate, the Bill returns to the Lords and ping-pong continues. Royal Assent has NOT been given. The Commons has agreed a carry-over motion giving the Bill until the end of 29 April 2027 to complete its remaining stages and receive Royal Assent, which means there is no near-term commencement date to plan against.

THE EVIDENCE CAVEAT MATTERS HERE MORE THAN USUAL, SO IT IS STATED FIRST. The report of yesterday's outcome rests on ONE non-official website, and that site's own page metadata is internally inconsistent with a 24 November event. No Hansard record and no parliament.uk Bill page could be read in this run. Do not brief the vote figures. Verify against Commons Hansard or the Bill's parliament.uk page before stating any outcome, and if your organisation has a parliamentary affairs function, this is a five-minute question for them.

THE TWO DISPUTED AMENDMENTS, AND WHY THEY MATTER DIFFERENTLY. The Lords added a register of foreign powers, at clause 67, which would require the Secretary of State to establish, within six months of Royal Assent, a register of foreign powers presenting a risk to UK critical systems. For a UK public body this is the amendment with operational consequences: a statutory register of risk-presenting foreign powers would feed directly into procurement decisions and supplier risk assessments, and its absence leaves those judgements where they are now, which is with individual organisations making them inconsistently. Amendment 163 would have required the Government to undertake and publish extensive reviews of the NIS regime within a year of Royal Assent - a transparency and accountability provision rather than an operational one.

WHAT IS ALREADY SETTLED, AND WHAT TO DO ABOUT IT. The vendor-direction powers in clauses 44 to 47 are not in dispute and will be in the Act. They allow direction of regulated entities in relation to their suppliers. The practical consequence is already clear and does not depend on the outcome of ping-pong: regulated bodies will need to know which third-party suppliers sit in their critical path. Most UK public bodies cannot currently state that. Build the inventory now. It is the same inventory that rank 9 of this report concludes is the only control that would have addressed four out of four UK retail and consumer incidents this month, which makes it the single action in this report that satisfies both a present risk and a known future legal obligation. Hold the detailed gap analysis until the final text is settled; do not hold the inventory.

THE PHP OUTAGES, ONE MONTH ON AND UNRESOLVED IN PUBLIC. On 22 October 2026 a technology minister told the House of Lords that 32 UK government services were unavailable and four partially unavailable as a result of critical PHP vulnerabilities, described as largely resulting from precautionary measures taken while security updates and mitigations were applied. The Government declined to publish a list of affected services on the basis that doing so is not standard practice, and stated in Hansard that it was not aware of any compromises in the UK public sector while acknowledging reports of exploitation activity in international scanning. Downing Street's position was that no large public-facing critical services were affected. Oxfordshire County Council and Hillingdon Council were among the councils that took systems offline to patch. More than 50,000 warnings were reported as sent to UK organisations.

No restoration update has been published in the month since, and none surfaced in this run. That absence is the finding, for two reasons. First, there is currently no public way to know whether those services are restored, whether they were restored by patching or by remaining offline, or whether any were found to be compromised after all. Second, and more usefully, those estates are the same estates that rank 1 of this report concerns. The organisations that could not quickly determine their PHP exposure in October are the organisations that cannot quickly determine today whether their Drupal installer is reachable. If you were one of the 32, the Drupal check at rank 1 is not a new task - it is the same task, on the same servers, with a KEV deadline on Thursday.

THE EXPIRED-DEADLINE BOARD. Carried forward so that nothing drops off a tracker silently: CVE-2026-123890, vCenter, deadline 23 November, PASSED - hunting open, SAML signing key decision open. CVE-2026-20320, BroadWorks, deadline 24 November, PASSED - three-month-old fix, key rotation outstanding. CVE-2026-124194, Outlook, deadline 24 November, PASSED - fix ships through the Office channel so Windows patch compliance reports green on a vulnerable estate; block outbound SMB on 445 as the compensating control. Cisco Expressway CVE-2026-76466, PASSED. And due in the next 48 hours: CVE-2026-133968 and CVE-2026-134624 tomorrow; CVE-2026-132165, CVE-2026-132224 and CVE-2026-131914 on Thursday. Five deadlines in two days, and none at all today.
recommended_actions: Verify yesterday's Cyber Security and Resilience Bill outcome against Commons Hansard or the Bill's page on parliament.uk before briefing anyone. The report that the Commons disagreed with both Lords amendments, including the 260 to 98 figure, rests on one non-official website whose own metadata is inconsistent with the date. Do not quote the vote figures.

Build the third-party supplier criticality inventory now, independent of the Bill's progress. The vendor-direction powers in clauses 44 to 47 are settled and will be in the Act, most UK public bodies cannot currently state which suppliers sit in their critical path, and the same inventory is the only control that addresses the four-for-four third-party pattern at rank 9.

Hold the detailed NIS gap analysis until the final text is settled, but do not hold the inventory. Royal Assent has not been given and the carry-over motion runs to 29 April 2027, so there is no commencement date to plan against - which is an argument for doing the durable preparatory work, not for doing nothing.

If you are a UK public body, ask internally whether you were among the 32 services taken offline in October for the PHP vulnerability, and if so, whether they were restored by patching or by remaining offline. There is no public answer, and the distinction determines whether you still have an exposure or merely an outage.

Treat the Drupal check at rank 1 as the same task on the same servers if you were affected by the PHP outages. The organisations that could not quickly determine their PHP exposure in October are the organisations that cannot determine their Drupal installer exposure today, and that one has a KEV deadline on Thursday.

Keep the expired KEV deadlines on your tracker with an explicit overdue status rather than letting them disappear when the date passes. CVE-2026-123890, CVE-2026-20320, CVE-2026-124194 and CVE-2026-76466 are all now overdue, and a silently dropped item is the most common route to invisible overdue remediation.

Fix the Outlook patch reporting gap permanently, not just for CVE-2026-124194. The fix ships through the Office update channel, so WSUS, Intune Windows rings and SCCM report green while every Outlook client stays vulnerable. Block outbound SMB on 445 as the compensating control and then address the reporting defect, because it will recur with the next Office vulnerability.

Plan for five KEV deadlines inside 48 hours and none today. Two expire tomorrow and three on Thursday. Decide today which you will miss and record the decision with a named owner - the ones that get missed are the ones nobody wrote down.

Note for your own threat model that the UK publicly confirmed offensive cyber operations against Russia, China, Iran and North Korea on 23 November. It is a single-source report with no operational detail, but it is a reasonable input to a discussion about retaliation risk for UK public bodies and critical infrastructure operators.

Where you have a parliamentary affairs or public policy function, give them a standing task to report the Bill's ping-pong outcomes rather than relying on threat intelligence collection for legislative status. This report's weakest evidence every week is the parliamentary item, and that is a sourcing problem with an easy internal fix.

kql.name: Public-facing software inventory for NIS scope and for the PHP question
kql.description: Serves both governance items at once. Produces the inventory the vendor-direction powers will require, and answers whether PHP and Drupal versions in your estate are the ones that were in scope in October.
kql.query:
DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory
| where SoftwareName has_any ("php", "drupal", "apache", "nginx", "iis", "wordpress", "tomcat")
| summarize Devices = dcount(DeviceId), DeviceList = make_set(DeviceName, 50), Versions = make_set(SoftwareVersion, 20) by SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName
| order by Devices desc

kql.name: Estate-wide view of the five KEV CVEs due in the next 48 hours
kql.description: The deadline tracker as a query. Produces the evidence of where each of the five outstanding items is present, and therefore where a missed deadline actually matters.
kql.query:
let KevNext48 = dynamic(["CVE-2026-133968", "CVE-2026-134624", "CVE-2026-132165", "CVE-2026-132224", "CVE-2026-131914"]);
let KevExpired = dynamic(["CVE-2026-123890", "CVE-2026-20320", "CVE-2026-124194", "CVE-2026-76466"]);
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where CveId in (KevNext48) or CveId in (KevExpired)
| extend Status = iff(CveId in (KevNext48), "DUE WITHIN 48H", "OVERDUE")
| summarize Devices = dcount(DeviceId), DeviceList = make_set(DeviceName, 40) by CveId, Status, SoftwareName, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel
| order by Status asc, Devices desc

kql.name: Microsoft Outlook build verification - the patch reporting gap
kql.description: The specific reason CVE-2026-124194's expired deadline is likely unmet: the fix ships through the Office channel, so Windows patch compliance reports green on a vulnerable estate. Check builds, not compliance.
kql.query:
DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory
| where SoftwareName has_any ("outlook", "office", "microsoft 365 apps")
| summarize Devices = dcount(DeviceId), Builds = make_set(SoftwareVersion, 30) by SoftwareName, SoftwareVendor
| order by Devices desc

kql.name: Outbound SMB on 445 - the Outlook compensating control
kql.description: Verifies that the compensating control for the overdue Outlook CVE is actually in place. CVE-2026-124194 leaks NTLMv2 hashes, so outbound SMB to the internet is the exposure, and this shows whether it is still possible.
kql.query:
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemotePort == 445
| where isnotempty(RemoteIP) and not(ipv4_is_private(RemoteIP))
| summarize Attempts = count(), Destinations = make_set(RemoteIP, 30), Processes = make_set(InitiatingProcessFileName, 15), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName
| order by Attempts desc

summary_statistics.window_assessment: A deadline-shaped window with one genuinely new high-consequence item for UK public sector. The structural fact is that no KEV deadline expires today while five expire within 48 hours, which makes today a triage day rather than a remediation day. The single most important finding is Drupal core CVE-2026-132165 at rank 1: an unauthenticated remote code execution flaw in a file that every Drupal site retains by default, that Drupal's own default .htaccess does not block, exploited on live sites about twenty-four hours after the fix shipped, with a KEV deadline on Thursday - sitting in exactly the UK local government, NHS and university web estates that frequently cannot name an owner for the sites concerned, and that were already the population taken offline in October for the PHP vulnerability with no restoration update published since. Three themes connect the rest. FIRST, the patch window has collapsed: Drupal was exploited in about a day, MONAI Label was taken to root in about eleven minutes, and the NCSC has now put its own name to the observation that familiar weaknesses are being exploited faster. The control implication is that asset discovery, not patch velocity, is the binding constraint - two of this report's worst items concern systems the owner did not know were reachable. SECOND, third-party compromise is now the dominant UK corporate pattern and it is four for four this month: Next through a supplier, ASOS through a communications platform, Optimizely through a vendor CDN, N-able through a vendor hosted platform. None of these was prevented by anything inside the victim's perimeter, and the Optimizely case specifically demonstrates that Content Security Policy allowlisting cannot distinguish a vendor from an attacker operating inside that vendor. THIRD, and now in its third week, automated vulnerability data keeps suppressing priority on exploited flaws: four entries in this report carry stale or conflicting tracker, NVD SSVC or vendor-PSIRT data that would cause a pipeline to under-prioritise an actively exploited vulnerability. For UK government specifically the highest-consequence item is a CMS installer nobody remembers leaving in place, the most likely hidden exposure remains an abandoned security library added on a reviewer's recommendation, and the one item with no detection path at all still has no CVE after a week.
summary_statistics.highest_priority_action: Eight things, in order, and the first takes one line of configuration. (1) BLOCK /core/install.php ON EVERY DRUPAL SITE YOU OWN, TODAY, BEFORE YOU FINISH THE INVENTORY. Drupal core CVE-2026-132165 lets an anonymous attacker drive the retained installer to site takeover and remote code execution. Drupal's default .htaccess does not block it, so assume it is reachable until you have requested it from outside and seen it blocked. Exploitation on live sites was reported from 19 November at 19:00 UTC, about a day after the 18 November fix, and the KEV deadline is Thursday 27 November. Then patch to 10.6.22, 11.3.22 or 11.4.13 - and for anything on 11.2.x or earlier, which is end of life and will never be fixed, make a migration decision this week rather than recording 'awaiting upgrade'. Find the sites with NCSC Web Check, not with the CMDB, because the ones nobody owns are the ones that will not get patched. (2) FIND OUT WHETHER YOU USE OPTIMIZELY WEB EXPERIMENTATION, AND ASK MARKETING, NOT IT. CVE-2026-132224 let an attacker abuse an unauthenticated signup flow to write JavaScript into at least 178 organisations' projects served from Optimizely's own CDN, skimming cards, swapping crypto addresses and attempting to load iPhone exploit kits, and it defeated the protections on the PCI-designated script host. Treat every card typed into a non-iframed field on an affected page on 16-17 November as potentially captured, notify your acquirer, and ask Optimizely in writing for your affected file list and your exact exposure window. Then take the architectural lesson: CSP helped nobody, because the code came from a host you had already allowlisted. (3) TWO KEV DEADLINES TOMORROW, AND NEITHER WILL BE FIXED BY THE PEOPLE READING THIS. MONAI Label CVE-2026-133968 is CVSS 9.8 with authentication OFF by default - patch to 0.8.6, enable authentication, and check sitecustomize.py on every server that ever ran it, because that is where Amazon documented the reverse shell and patching does not remove a file the attacker already wrote. Ask research computing and imaging teams directly; these servers are not in your inventory, and that is the finding. N-able Mail Assure CVE-2026-134624 reaches UK organisations through MSPs, so send your MSP a written question today - what build, was our tenant in scope, and was this the entry vector for the 16 November breach - and do not accept 'confined to a single hosted server' as an answer to the second. (4) SEARCH EVERY IIS SERVER FOR Idunno.AntiCsrf.dll, AND NOTE THE CORRECTION: CVE-2026-131914 WAS ADDED TO KEV YESTERDAY, due Thursday. This feed said it was not listed. There is now a mandated remediation date for a flaw with no patch and no maintainer, which means the only compliant remediation is deleting the DLL and its Web.config registration. Internet-facing first, WAF rule as the interim, and do not rotate machine keys and call it fixed - reporting is explicit that it changes nothing. (5) READ THE NCSC BLOG AND ACT ON TWO LINES OF IT. 'Familiar weaknesses, exploited faster', published 24 November, confirms a marked rise in AI-assisted attacks since September and names six agentic frameworks. Its central finding is that nothing new is being exploited, only faster - which removes the excuse rather than adding a procurement item. Two recommendations earn immediate work: move rate limiting from source addresses to accounts and tokens, and throttle unauthenticated signup flows while checking what a brand-new unverified account can reach. That second one is the exact gap that produced item (2) above. (6) CHECK WHETHER YOUR vCENTER TICKET SAYS VMSA-2026-0009 OR VMSA-2026-0011. If it says 0009 you have an open CVSS 9.8 authentication bypass, CVE-2026-123903, in the same vmdir component the Armory Castle zero-day chain abused - and a second independent bypass in that component is the argument for finally closing the SAML STS signing key rotation decision, because an attacker holding that material mints valid assertions indefinitely and no password reset revokes it. Patch to 9.1.2, 9.0.2.0300 or 8.0 U3m, and assume there is no workaround. (7) IF YOU RUN AZURE API MANAGEMENT CLASSIC, ROTATION PROGRESS IS YOUR ONLY STATUS - DAY SEVEN. Still no CVE, still no public advisory, still no customer-visible log, still no way to prove you were not accessed, and Microsoft's fix still does not invalidate what was already stolen. Named Values first, then identity provider secrets, then subscription keys, then management tokens. Keep the Named Value to backend map it forces you to build. (8) AND RUN THE ONE-COMMAND SEARCH: grep erlang.log on every Cisco Expressway node for wombat@127.0.0.1. It is the only hard indicator in this entire report. Then do the part everybody skips - audit internal GitLab for committed credentials and rotate what you find, because the Expressway intrusion harvested repositories and those credentials survive every patch you apply to the appliance. Two governance notes. The Cyber Security and Resilience Bill did NOT receive Royal Assent and reportedly went back to the Lords yesterday, but that report is single-source and unverified so do not brief the vote figures - build the third-party supplier criticality inventory anyway, because the vendor-direction powers in clauses 44 to 47 are settled and the same inventory is the only control that would have addressed four out of four UK third-party incidents this month. And one month on, nobody has published whether the 32 UK government services taken offline for the PHP flaw are back - if you were one of them, the Drupal check in item (1) is the same task on the same servers.
